title: Knowledge-rich curricula: A key driver of equity in education collection,
author: Dylan Wiliam
source: Dylan Wiliam on Substack (originally in The value of a knowledge-rich curriculum: An essay
summary: Wiliam takes the twenty-five-year-old OECD case for generic skills over content and demolishes it on cognitive-science grounds. The argument that transferable skills like critical thinking, creativity, and problem solving can be taught as stand-alone competencies sounds attractive because it promises portability across any context, including contexts that do not yet exist. The evidence is that it does not work, and the reason it does not work is not implementation failure but a model of human thinking that is wrong at the foundation. Minds perform as well as they do because they are huge stores of information, and working memory can only operate on what is already in long-term memory. The piece walks through three concrete examples that make the point without a single reference to cognitive load theory. Copying five Cyrillic characters takes multiple glances unless you happen to know Kazakh. An eleven-digit phone number is impossible to hold unless you happen to recognise 02920 as the Cardiff dialling code. A Countdown-style number puzzle solves itself if you happen to know that twenty-five times four is a hundred. In each case, the person with the relevant knowledge in long-term memory is not smarter, they just have more to think with. Wiliam then extends the claim to the supposedly generic skills themselves: training pupils to think critically in history has no measurable transfer to mathematics, and creativity, properly defined, is making novel selections from well-stocked shelves. The equity consequence is the one primary teachers most need to hear. When France and Sweden drifted from systematic knowledge-building toward generic skills, the achievement gap between pupils from more and less affluent homes widened, because children in affluent homes were picking up the necessary background knowledge at the dinner table. The Hirsch cricket paragraph is the textbook case: fluent readers lacking the background cannot make the right sense of the passage. Wiliam closes with a clean instruction for practice. Curate coherent, cumulative bodies of knowledge across the whole curriculum, teach them with high expectations and effective pedagogy, and skills will flourish where knowledge is abundant, not in the vacuum where they are typically taught.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Attempts to do this in the past, such as the thinking skills programmes that were popular in England 20 years ago, failed to yield any significant benefits. In response, supporters of such programmes argued that the failures were caused by inadequate implementation, and if only the programmes had been implemented properly, they would have worked.

These three examples reveal an important insight into the way that human minds work; namely, that it is the information that we have in long-term memory that determines what we can do. Some people say that it is not necessary to learn multiplication facts, provided that you understand the principles. For example, they say that if a pupil does not know what 6 times 6 is, but knows that 3 times 6 is 18 and can double this to get 36, then that’s OK, but it really isn’t.

The way we make our children smarter is not by giving them practice in thinking. We need to give them more to think with. We make our pupils smarter by increasing the knowledge they have in their heads.

However, no amount of training pupils to think critically in history has any impact on their ability to think critically in mathematics. Critical thinking is a bundle of superficially similar skills that rely on fundamentally different cognitive processes.

Someone once described creativity as making novel selections from well-stocked shelves, and that is why creativity requires having a lot of knowledge about the field in which one wants to be creative.

American readers would struggle to make sense of this, not because they are unfamiliar with the words used, but because they lack the background knowledge to understand what the paragraph is describing. A lack of background knowledge makes it hard to make sense of what one is reading, but often also means that the sense that one does make is not, in fact, correct.
